items.name: PEP
items.kind: Productivity Enhancement Platform · HR suite · Enterprise UX
items.blurb: Connecting four HR workflows through one platform model, with candidate comparison prioritized over a board-first recruitment view.
items.summary: PEP covers the employee lifecycle — hiring, attendance, growth and feedback — built so learning one module teaches you the rest.
items.problem: Hiring, attendance, learning and feedback describe one person, but ran as four systems that disagreed. Training was paid for four times.
items.solve: Designed the shell before the screens: one module rail, one workspace, one list-record-edit pattern. Modules fit the frame rather than negotiating with each other.
did: Led the design team building the platform, from requirements gathering through final designs.
Defined the shared shell — module rail, global search, documents/announcement/report bar — that every module inherits.
Designed the four flagship modules: recruitment, time and attendance, learning and development, employee engagement.
Ran weekly reviews against the shell so consistency was a condition of delivery, not a matter of taste.
Rebuilt the design as an interactive coded prototype to show flows, states and validation for engineering handoff.

sections.label: Problem
sections.title: One employee lifecycle, four unrelated products
paras: Hiring, attendance, training and feedback are one continuous story about a person. In most organisations they are four systems that disagree about navigation, record editing and what a destructive action looks like.
The cost lands on the HR administrator who has to work across all four, and on training every new one of them.

points.head: The shell is the product
points.body: If the frame holds, a new module is a content problem rather than a design problem.

sections.label: Philosophy
sections.title: Design the frame, and the screens design themselves
paras: Enterprise products fail as a collection, not as screens. Each module is defensible on its own and the sum is unlearnable — so I spend the early time on the shell and the vocabulary rather than on any one page.

The test I hold myself to: can a new module be specified by describing its content, because its layout, navigation and destructive-action pattern are already decided? If the answer is no, the system is not finished, however good the individual screens look.

points.head: What I optimise for
points.body: The cost of learning the second module after the first.

points.head: Density is not the enemy
points.body: Operators compare rows for a living. I fight clutter, not information.

sections.label: Recruitment
sections.title: A candidate pipeline you can actually work from
paras: The candidates view is a dense, sortable table by design: name, contact, role, internal or external, CGPA, CV, applied date, graduation date, social profiles. Recruiters compare rows; hiding columns to look calmer just moves the work into clicks.
Filters sit above the table for the three cuts that get used — date range, job, department, stage — and the primary action is adding candidates, because that is why the screen gets opened.

images.cap: Recruitment — the candidate pipeline

tradeoffs.old: The first pipeline was a kanban of stages — visually clearer, and it demoed beautifully. Recruiters working eight candidates at a time needed to compare attributes side by side, which columns do and cards cannot.
tradeoffs.now: A table as the default view, with stage as a filter. Less impressive in a demo, faster in the job.

sections.label: Attendance
sections.title: Attendance is a record, so show the whole record
paras: The attendance view pairs leave balances and history with a per-day detail: clock in, clock out, lunch, breaks, with lateness stated inline against the entry it describes rather than summarised elsewhere.
Overtime, total time, status and who imported the record are all on the same screen — because the reason anyone opens this page is a dispute about one specific day.

points.head: Exceptions in place
points.body: A late mark next to the timestamp it refers to, not in a summary column.

images.cap: Time & attendance — leave balances, history and day detail

sections.label: Learning
sections.title: Employee growth through structured learning
paras: The learning module presents a course as a lesson sequence with the video, the written detail, attachments, and a single forward action — Complete — so progress through a curriculum is unambiguous.
Training management, needs analysis and personal growth plans sit in the same rail, so an employee and an administrator navigate the same structure from different ends.

images.cap: Learning & development — a lesson in a course sequence

sections.label: Engagement
sections.title: Feedback is only useful when it is actionable
paras: Surveys are cards carrying two numbers that matter — how much is filled, and how much is resolved. Completion without resolution is the failure mode of every engagement programme, so both are on the card.
Creating a survey is the primary action, and department and status filters keep a large programme navigable.

images.cap: Employee engagement — surveys with filled and resolved rates

sections.label: Outcome
sections.title: Four modules that read as one platform
paras: The modules ship on a shared shell, so an administrator who learns recruitment can work attendance without retraining, and the next module can be specified by its content rather than its layout.

images.cap: PEP across devices

pm.audience: HR administrators, recruiters and employees navigating the employee lifecycle.
pm.opportunity: Keep hiring, attendance, learning and engagement connected so each module does not require a different way of working.
pm.decision: Define the shared platform shell before expanding the four modules.
pm.tradeoff: A recruitment table supports comparing candidate attributes; a kanban makes stage movement more visual. The documented decision favored comparison, with stage available as a filter.
pm.hypothesis: If the modules share navigation and record patterns, administrators should be able to transfer what they learn in one module to the next.
pm.evidence: The portfolio records a shipped HR platform, four designed modules and shared interaction patterns. It does not provide a measured reduction in training or task time.
metrics: Recruiter task completion and time to compare candidates
First-task success when moving to a second module
Support requests about navigation and module differences
pm.learning: Platform consistency is a product scope decision: new modules should inherit the shared model before introducing exceptions.
pm.caption: Recruitment management: candidate comparison and stage filtering.

items.heroCaption: Recruitment management: candidate comparison and stage filtering.
items.prototypeNote: This is the PEP design rebuilt from the Figma file as a working prototype: 22 screens across recruitment, attendance, learning, engagement, OKRs and payroll. It shows how I prefer to hand work to engineering. Instead of static frames, developers can click through real flows, filters, empty states and validation, so questions get answered before build rather than during it. Try it below.

items.name: Enterprise CRM
items.kind: CRM platform · Seven roles · Enterprise UX
items.blurb: Defining a shared CRM across seven roles, with useful role-specific defaults before dashboard customization.
items.summary: A CRM built around seven roles: sales reps working leads, marketing running campaigns, support handling tickets, branch managers approving requests, directors reading performance, and a customer portal.
items.problem: Sales ran on spreadsheets, marketing measured campaigns by feel, and directors built strategy from reports that were already out of date.
items.solve: One data model — contact, lead, pipeline, campaign, ticket, target — with seven interfaces onto it. Each role sees only what it can act on, and reporting rolls up automatically.
items.poster: Seven roles. One source of truth.
did: Ran the UX research: four primary personas across sales, marketing, branch management and the executive level, with journey maps and a competitive analysis.
Defined the information architecture and role model — which of the seven roles sees, edits and approves what.
Designed every module across seven role-based interfaces plus a customer portal, an e-learning module, the authentication set and a public landing page.
Built the design system that holds it together: tokens, fields, tables, kanban cards, modals, navigation and a rich-text editor.
Designed against WCAG contrast from the start — the gap the competitive analysis found in every rival product.

sections.label: Problem
sections.title: Seven roles, seven versions of the truth
paras: The organisation ran its customer relationships on manual tools. Sales representatives tracked leads in spreadsheets and notebooks. Marketing segmented audiences by hand in Excel and could not measure a campaign’s return. Branch managers approved work over messages and reported upward from figures that were out of date before they were sent. Directors assembled strategy from whatever arrived.

None of these are separate problems. They are one problem — nobody shares an object — reappearing in four job descriptions. Every role was re-entering data another role already had, and each re-entry was a chance for the numbers to diverge.

points.head: Manual everywhere
points.body: Spreadsheets for leads, Excel for segments, messages for approvals.

points.head: Reporting as archaeology
points.body: Managers reconstructed the week instead of reading it.

points.head: No lead-to-revenue line
points.body: Nobody could trace a closed deal back to the campaign that started it.

sections.label: Philosophy
sections.title: One model, seven windows
paras: A CRM is not an application; it is an agreement about what a customer is. Once seven roles agree on the objects — contact, lead, pipeline stage, campaign, ticket, target — the interfaces stop competing and become views. Get that wrong and you ship seven products that argue with each other at the end of every quarter.

So I designed the role model before the screens: what each role can see, edit, assign and approve. A sales representative should never meet a branch-level approval control; a director should never be asked to work a single lead. Permission is not a settings page — it is the shape of the interface.

The second commitment was that reporting must be a by-product. If a manager has to ask someone to compile a number, the system has failed regardless of how good the dashboard looks. Every figure a director reads is a consequence of work someone already did in their own view.

points.head: What I optimise for
points.body: The number of times the same fact gets typed in — target one.

points.head: Permission as layout
points.body: Roles differ by what they can act on, not by a toggle in settings.

points.head: Reporting is downstream
points.body: No figure exists because someone was asked to produce it.

sections.label: Research
sections.title: Four people who all wanted the same thing differently
paras: The research centred on four personas built from interviews. Meron Mehari, a sales representative, wants to close more deals and stop tracking leads in a notebook — she needs a visual pipeline and automated reminders, and she is nervous about learning a new system after years of manual process. Bethel Nigussie, a marketing specialist, wants to digitise campaign planning and finally measure return; her blocker is that marketing and sales follow-up are not connected at all.

Biniam Solomon, a branch manager, wants to monitor team performance in real time and stop chasing approvals — his risk is being overwhelmed by reporting detail rather than helped by it. Tadesse Girma, a director, wants consolidated KPIs across branches and regions, and is sceptical about the platform’s return on investment.

The journey maps repeated one shape across all four: discovery is easy, adoption is where it dies. Every persona surfaced the same anxieties — the learning curve, the time cost of changing workflow, whether the dashboards can be tailored to their actual job. That is a design problem, not a training problem, and it is why role-specific defaults matter more than configurability.

points.head: Meron — sales representative
points.body: Visual pipeline, real-time prioritisation, reminders. Fears the learning curve.

points.head: Bethel — marketing specialist
points.body: Segmentation, campaign ROI, a real handoff to sales.

points.head: Biniam — branch manager
points.body: Team performance at a glance, faster approvals, fewer stale reports.

points.head: Tadesse — director
points.body: Consolidated KPIs across branches; needs the ROI argument made.

tradeoffs.old: The first response to "dashboards must be customisable" was a configurable widget grid — every role builds their own view. It answers the request literally and hands a new user an empty canvas on day one.
tradeoffs.now: Pre-configured dashboards per role, tailored to that persona’s journey, with customisation available afterwards. The research was explicit: people wanted immediate insight, not a builder.

sections.label: Role model
sections.title: Seven roles, defined before a single screen was drawn
paras: Before any interface existed I wrote the roles down: what each one is responsible for, and what the system will let them do. Sales representatives own leads and quotes. Marketing owns campaigns and segments. Support owns tickets and the knowledge base. Branch managers approve plans and watch a team. Directors set targets and read across branches. System administrators own users, roles and configuration.

This is the document the whole product hangs from — and the reason permission never became a settings screen. If a director can approve a regional plan and a representative cannot, that difference shows up as the presence or absence of a control, not as a greyed-out button explaining what you are not allowed to do.

Writing responsibilities and permissions side by side also caught the mismatches early: every case where someone was accountable for a number they had no way to affect, or could change something they were not answerable for.

points.head: Responsibility first
points.body: Each role starts as a list of what it owns, not a list of screens.

points.head: Permission as presence
points.body: You see the controls you can act on. Nothing is shown to be denied.

points.head: Caught early
points.body: Accountability without authority is a design bug — the role sheets surface it.

images.cap: Sales representative — responsibilities and permissions.
Marketing specialist — campaign ownership and segment access.
Customer support — ticket ownership and escalation rights.
Customer support, continued — knowledge base and feedback duties.
Branch manager — approvals, team monitoring and local targets.
Director — branch leaderboard, regional approvals, forecasting.
System administrator — users, roles, configuration and logs.

sections.label: Competitive analysis
sections.title: Benchmarked against the tools already in use
paras: I compared the platform against the incumbent CRMs across eight axes: lead management, pipeline customisation, project management, invoicing and payment tracking, reporting and analytics, user interface, scalability, accessibility and customer support tooling.

The pattern was consistent. The powerful tools were overwhelming for beginners; the friendly ones had a limited visual pipeline and shallow reporting. And on accessibility, the field was empty — no competitor treated WCAG compliance as a requirement. That became a deliberate differentiator rather than a compliance checkbox: readable type sizes, contrast-checked colour pairs, and no state signalled by colour alone.

points.head: The gap I designed into
points.body: Advanced lead management with a clean UI — the axis nobody held both ends of.

points.head: Accessibility as position
points.body: No competitor claimed WCAG. We did, from the first screen.

sections.label: Sales
sections.title: A pipeline you can see and a lead you can work
paras: The sales representative is the heaviest user, so their surface sets the vocabulary for the rest. The dashboard opens on what needs attention today — targets, tasks, the deals closest to moving — rather than on statistics about last month.

Leads live in a table you can actually work: sortable, filterable, with score, stage and owner visible without opening anything. The lead detail is the piece I spent longest on. Everything a follow-up needs sits under one header — activity, call log, emails, notes, documents, scoring — as tabs on the same record rather than pages you navigate between, because a representative on a call cannot afford to lose their place.

points.head: Today, not last month
points.body: The dashboard is a work queue with targets attached.

points.head: One record, many tabs
points.body: Calls, emails, notes, files and score never leave the lead.

sections.label: Marketing
sections.title: A campaign that knows what happened to its leads
paras: Marketing’s problem was not tooling, it was the gap after the send. The campaign builder therefore treats audience, content and measurement as one object: you segment, compose, schedule and define what success means in the same flow, so the campaign carries its own definition of return.

Because segments are built from the same contact records sales works in, a lead generated by a campaign stays attributable through the pipeline. That single connection is what turns marketing from a cost centre into something a director can read.

points.head: One flow
points.body: Audience, content, schedule and success criteria defined together.

points.head: Attribution by construction
points.body: Segments are contact records, so the lead keeps its origin.

sections.label: Support
sections.title: A ticket is a promise with a name on it
paras: Support was designed on the same principle I use for any case system: an issue that exists without an owner and a deadline is not being managed, it is being stored. Every ticket carries a category, an assignee, a priority and a status that reads as a word — and the queue is ordered by what is at risk rather than by what arrived last.

The customer portal is the other half. Customers see their own tickets, order history, quotes and loyalty standing, and can search a knowledge base before opening a ticket at all — which is the cheapest support the platform offers.

points.head: Ownership at intake
points.body: Category, assignee and priority set when the ticket is created.

points.head: Self-service first
points.body: A knowledge base in front of the queue, not buried behind it.

sections.label: Administration
sections.title: The role model made operable
paras: Everything the role sheets promised has to be administrable by someone, so the system administrator gets a surface of their own: user directory, role definitions, configuration, logs and the platform-wide report view.

The users table carries the four facts an administrator acts on — who, what role, active or not, since when — and nothing else. Role management is where the permission model stops being a document and becomes state: create a role, define what it can reach, and every interface in the product reshapes itself accordingly.

points.head: Roles are data
points.body: Permission lives in the role record, not in seven hard-coded interfaces.

points.head: Four facts per user
points.body: Identity, role, status, tenure — the columns an admin actually acts on.

images.cap: System administrator — user counts, activity trend and the user directory.
Role management — where the permission model becomes editable state.

sections.label: E-learning
sections.title: The answer to the adoption problem the research found
paras: Every persona named the same fear: the learning curve. Training is usually answered with a PDF and a workshop, both of which happen once and then decay. So onboarding was built into the platform as an e-learning module — courses, lessons and progress living where the work lives.

The course builder is deliberately plain: title, description, structure, media, publish. It has to be usable by a branch manager writing a twenty-minute induction, not only by a training department. That is what keeps the material current after launch — the people who know the process can edit it without filing a request.

points.head: Training as a feature
points.body: Onboarding inside the product, not a document beside it.

points.head: Authored by the operators
points.body: Anyone who owns a process can maintain its course.

points.head: Progress is visible
points.body: A manager sees who has completed what, without asking.

images.cap: E-learning — course catalogue with progress per learner.
Course detail — lessons, materials and completion state.
Course creation — structure and content in one plain form.
Course creation, continued — lessons and media.

sections.label: Authentication
sections.title: The first screen is a trust screen
paras: Sign-in is the one surface every role meets, usually while distracted, sometimes while locked out. I designed the full set rather than the happy path: sign in, recover, confirm recovery, and the confirmation state — each one saying plainly what just happened and what to do next.

Recovery gets the same care as sign-in because the moment a person cannot get in is the moment the platform feels least trustworthy. No dead ends, no unexplained errors, and a confirmation that states the outcome in a sentence.

points.head: The whole set
points.body: Sign in, recover, confirm, done — states, not just a form.

points.head: Every message plain
points.body: What happened, and the one thing to do next.

images.cap: Sign in — the one screen all seven roles share.
Account recovery.
Recovery confirmation — outcome stated in a sentence.
Confirmation state.

sections.label: Design system
sections.title: Seven interfaces that had to stay one product
paras: Seven roles designed by a team over months will diverge unless the system is stricter than the schedule. I built the foundations as Figma variables — a deep navy and blue brand ramp, neutral greys tuned for dense tables, semantic status colours — and documented every component as a variant set: fields in each case and state, buttons across style and size, tables, kanban cards, modals, navigation, steppers, checkboxes, toggles and a full rich-text editor toolbar.

Density is the only axis the roles are allowed to differ on. The sales table tightens; the customer portal breathes. What never changes is the meaning of a colour, the anatomy of a field or where the primary action sits — which is what let seven interfaces ship as one product.

points.head: Variables, not swatches
points.body: Tokens across colour, spacing and type the whole team built against.

points.head: Every state documented
points.body: Fields, buttons and tables drawn in the conditions they actually meet.

points.head: WCAG in the tokens
points.body: Contrast checked at the token level, so no screen could quietly fail it.

sections.label: Outcome
sections.title: A platform seven roles could adopt without a rewrite
paras: The work delivered the full product definition: research, personas, journey maps, competitive analysis, information architecture, wireframes, seven role-based interfaces, a customer portal, a public landing page and the design system underneath them — handed over role by role so engineering could build in the order the business needed.

The premise it defends is unglamorous: most CRM failures are adoption failures, and adoption is decided by whether the interface matches the job. Every role-specific default in this product exists because the research said the same thing four times — give me my work, not a configuration screen.

points.head: Shipped as a handover
points.body: Seven role packages, a design system and the reasoning attached.

points.head: What I would watch
points.body: Adoption per role in month one — the number the research says decides it.

pm.audience: Sales, marketing, support, branch management and executive teams.
pm.opportunity: Give each role actionable information while preserving a shared model for customer records, ownership and reporting.
pm.decision: Lead with role-specific dashboards rather than asking new users to configure a blank widget grid.
pm.tradeoff: Flexible configuration offers control, but increases setup work. The documented approach provides useful defaults first and customization afterward.
pm.hypothesis: If each role starts with the work and information it needs, users should reach useful insight with less configuration.
pm.evidence: Research, personas, journey maps, competitive analysis, a seven-role model and engineering handover are documented. Adoption and revenue impact are not quantified.
metrics: Time to first meaningful action for each role
Completion of lead follow-up and support workflows
Role-level adoption and reporting discrepancies
pm.learning: The shared data model and role boundaries need to be decided together; interface customization cannot resolve unclear ownership.
pm.caption: Administration workspace: user access, roles and reporting in one view.
pm.discovery: Research, personas, journey maps and a competitive analysis came first, which led to a seven-role model that shaped every dashboard.

items.name: Complaint Management
items.kind: Case management · Service operations · Enterprise UX
items.blurb: Making service accountability explicit through ownership and SLAs, with separate surfaces for agent work and management decisions.
items.summary: A workspace for resolving complaints: a reporting dashboard, a working ticket queue, a category and SLA model that routes each case to the right unit, and a knowledge base.
items.problem: Complaints were logged and then went quiet — no owner, no deadline, and a complainant left guessing. That is how a fixable problem becomes an escalation.
items.solve: Modelled the complaint itself — category, service unit, SLA in hours — so routing and deadlines exist before anyone opens the queue. The dashboard and knowledge base build on the same model.
did: Designed the complaint lifecycle end to end: intake, categorisation, assignment, resolution and reporting.
Built the analytics dashboard around the five numbers a service manager is accountable for.
Designed the category and SLA model that routes a complaint to the right unit automatically.
Designed the knowledge base authoring experience so answers become reusable instead of retyped.

sections.label: Problem
sections.title: Complaints get received, then lost
paras: Most organisations are good at receiving a complaint and bad at the twenty days that follow. It arrives by phone, email or in person, gets written somewhere, and its status becomes whatever the person who took it remembers.
The complainant experiences that as silence, which is what turns a resolvable problem into an escalation.

points.head: Ownership decays
points.body: A case with no named owner is a case nobody is late on.

points.head: Silence is the failure
points.body: People forgive slow resolution far more readily than no news.

sections.label: Philosophy
sections.title: Fix the model, not the screen
paras: When an operation is failing, the request is almost always for a better dashboard. But a queue can only show what the data knows — if a complaint has no category, no owning unit and no promised deadline, no layout will make it accountable.

So I treat the data model as the primary design surface. Get category, service unit and SLA right and the queue, the reporting and the escalation rules all fall out of it. Get them wrong and every screen becomes a workaround.

points.head: What I optimise for
points.body: Cases that cannot exist in an ambiguous state.

points.head: Where the design lives
points.body: In three fields nobody photographs for a portfolio.

sections.label: Starting point
sections.title: The work was already happening in a generic helpdesk
paras: Before the redesign, complaints ran through an off-the-shelf support desk. It handled tickets competently and knew nothing about complaints: no service unit, no category-level SLA, no distinction between a question and a grievance a regulator might ask about.
So the brief was not "build a ticket tool". It was to model the complaint itself — its category, its owning unit, its promised resolution time — and let the queue fall out of that.

points.head: What carried over
points.body: Status, priority, assignee and a scannable list. Those patterns were working and stayed.

points.head: What was missing
points.body: Category, service unit and SLA — the three fields that make a complaint different from a ticket.

sections.label: The queue
sections.title: Saved views are the product for an agent
paras: An agent never wants "all tickets". They want the four cuts that describe their obligations, so the rail carries them as counted views: all tickets, my open tickets, unassigned, overdue, closed and spam — plus custom views for high priority and customer follow-ups.
The counts are the point. Unassigned and overdue with a number beside them turn two silent failure modes into something a supervisor can see from the sidebar without opening anything.

points.head: Unassigned is a state, not an oversight
points.body: A named view means nobody has to remember to check for orphaned cases.

points.head: Overdue is separate from open
points.body: Breaching a promise is a different problem from having work in progress.

points.head: Row scanning
points.body: Ticket ID, subject, customer, status, priority, assignee, last update — one line per case, in reading order.

sections.label: Platform
sections.title: What sits behind the queue
paras: The system is not only an agent tool. The rail carries the administrative surfaces a service operation actually needs: setup, unit management, human resource, customer management, report and analytics, and the knowledge base.
Grouping them into one shell is what lets a category point at a service unit, a unit point at its people, and a report cover all of them — the joins that make the reporting trustworthy.

points.head: Unit management
points.body: Service units are the routing target and the reporting dimension.

points.head: Customer management
points.body: The complainant is a record with a history, not a name on a ticket.

points.head: Report & analytics
points.body: Reporting reads the same model the queue writes to, so numbers reconcile.

sections.label: Dashboard
sections.title: Five numbers a service manager is answerable for
paras: The dashboard leads with volume, open load, resolved count, resolution rate and average resolution time — each with its movement against the previous week, because a rate without a direction tells you nothing.

Below that, three views answer the three questions that follow: is the backlog growing (received against resolved over time), are we responding fast enough (average first reply), and where is the volume coming from (channel breakdown). Customer satisfaction closes the page with its trend and full distribution rather than a single average, so a rise in "very dissatisfied" cannot hide inside a healthy mean.

points.head: The five headline metrics
points.body: Total complaints, open, resolved, resolution rate and average resolution time — each with a week-on-week delta and its direction.

points.head: Channel mix
points.body: Email, web portal, mobile app, phone and social as one donut with counts, so an investment argument has a number behind it.

points.head: CSAT in full
points.body: The five-point distribution sits beside the average — the tail is the story a mean hides.

points.head: Honest footnote
points.body: The page states CSAT is collected after resolution, so the score is never over-read.

points.head: One date range, one filter
points.body: Every panel obeys the range at the top. No panel-level time controls to disagree with each other.

images.cap: Analytics dashboard — headline metrics, trends, channel mix and CSAT

tradeoffs.old: An earlier dashboard opened on the complaint queue — the argument being that managers should see live work first. It made the page a second inbox, and nobody used it for the decision it existed to support.
tradeoffs.now: The dashboard reports, the queue works. Separating them meant the manager view could answer "is this getting better or worse" without competing with the agent view.

sections.label: Categories & SLA
sections.title: Routing is a data model, not a rule engine
paras: A category is where the promise gets made: a name, the responsible service unit, a default priority and an SLA target in hours. Define those once and every complaint of that type routes to the right team with a deadline already attached.

The form explains itself as you fill it — why categories exist, what better organisation and faster resolution buy you, and a note that categories can be deactivated later. Configuration screens are used rarely and by people under pressure, so the reasoning belongs on the page rather than in a manual.

points.head: SLA at the category
points.body: The deadline is a property of the complaint type, stated in hours, so no case arrives without one.

points.head: Service unit, not person
points.body: Routing to a team survives staff turnover; routing to an individual does not.

points.head: Default priority
points.body: Set per category, overridable per case — the common path needs no decision.

points.head: Attachments allowed
points.body: Policy documents can sit with the category that enforces them.

points.head: Deactivate, never delete
points.body: Retiring a category preserves the history reported against it.

images.cap: Create complaint category — service unit, priority and SLA target

sections.label: Knowledge base
sections.title: Answer once, reuse forever
paras: The same complaints recur, and the cost of retyping an answer is paid every time by whoever is fastest at typing. Article authoring is therefore a first-class surface: title, slug, category, visibility, summary and a rich-text body, with templates for how-to guides, FAQs, policies and troubleshooting.

Visibility is the field that makes it work in both directions — the same article can serve an agent internally and a customer in self-service, which is what stops the knowledge base becoming a second, staler copy of itself.

points.head: Templates over blank pages
points.body: How-to guide, FAQ, policy and troubleshooting — because "write an article" is the reason nothing gets written.

points.head: One article, two audiences
points.body: Visibility decides who sees it; the content stays single-sourced.

points.head: Slug and summary as fields
points.body: A 160-character summary and an explicit URL slug make articles findable outside the tool, not just inside it.

points.head: Editor, then preview
points.body: Formatting kept to what support answers need — emphasis, lists, quotes, code, images.

images.cap: Create new article — metadata, editor and starting templates

sections.label: Reflection
sections.title: The model did the work the queue got credit for
paras: Every improvement people noticed — cases arriving at the right team, deadlines that exist before anyone looks, reporting that adds up — came from getting category, service unit and SLA right as data, not from anything on the queue screen.
It is the least visible part of the design and the part I would spend the time on again.

pm.audience: Service agents, service managers and people submitting complaints.
pm.opportunity: Make complaint ownership and deadlines visible from intake through resolution.
pm.decision: Separate the manager’s analytics dashboard from the agent’s working queue.
pm.tradeoff: Opening on live cases makes the dashboard another inbox. Separating reporting from queue work gives each role a clearer decision surface.
pm.hypothesis: If complaints carry category, service-unit ownership and an SLA from intake, teams should be able to identify overdue work and act before escalation.
pm.evidence: The documented scope covers intake, routing, SLAs, a working queue, analytics and a knowledge base. No measured SLA or resolution-time improvement is supplied.
metrics: Percentage of cases assigned to an owner
SLA compliance and median resolution time
Repeat contacts, reopen rate and escalation volume
pm.learning: Accountability starts with the complaint model; dashboard charts become useful only when ownership and status data are dependable.
pm.caption: Service analytics: a management view distinct from the agent queue.

items.name: Rad Reader
items.blurb: Connecting clinics and radiologists through a clear diagnostic handoff, with a queue-first workspace and dedicated study viewer.
items.summary: Three connected products — a patient app, a health-centre console and a radiologist workspace — for sending radiology scans out for expert reading.
items.problem: Ethiopia has far more scans than radiologists, and most specialists work in a handful of urban hospitals. A rural clinic can capture a CT with no one to read it.
items.solve: Separated capture from interpretation. Clinics upload the study and its context, radiologists read from a shared queue, and the patient tracks the case and gets the report.
did: Ran the UX research: three primary personas, journey maps across awareness, consideration and decision, competitive analysis and preference testing.
Designed the full product architecture — patient mobile app, health-centre console, radiologist workspace and admin side — as one platform.
Designed every screen across the three surfaces: upload, scan viewer, comparison, result writing, payment and history.
Built the design system: purple brand ramp, typography, icon set, form fields, tables, steppers and status components.
Wrote the product overview — purpose, audience, market need, feature set and roadmap — used to align the product and software teams.

sections.label: Problem
sections.title: The scanner is not the bottleneck. The reader is.
paras: Radiology is the most resource-intensive part of diagnostic medicine: the equipment is expensive to buy and maintain, the training pipeline is long, and the specialists who can read a complex study are concentrated in a few urban centres. A clinic in a regional town can own a machine and still have nobody qualified to interpret what it produces.

The consequence is a queue that nobody manages. Studies wait for a visiting radiologist, physicians make provisional calls under time pressure, and patients travel to the capital for a reading rather than for treatment. The cost lands on the people least able to absorb it.

points.head: Specialist scarcity
points.body: Too few radiologists, unevenly distributed and expensive to retain per centre.

points.head: Urban concentration
points.body: Access to interpretation depends on where the patient happens to live.

points.head: Time as harm
points.body: In radiology a slow answer is not an inconvenience; it changes the treatment.

sections.label: Philosophy
sections.title: Design the handoff, not the app
paras: Three roles touch a single study — the health centre that captures it, the radiologist who reads it, and the patient it belongs to. Each has a different competence, a different device and a different reason to open the product. The temptation is to design three apps; the mistake is to let them disagree about what a case is.

So I treated the handoff as the primary design object. A study carries its own context — modality, patient history, urgency, who is assigned, what has been said about it — and each interface is a view onto that same object shaped for one role’s job. When the object is right, the three products stay honest with each other without anybody coordinating.

The second principle was medical restraint. This is not a product that should feel clever. Every screen states what is known, what is pending, and who holds it next; nothing important is inferred, animated, or hidden behind a gesture.

points.head: What I optimise for
points.body: Hours from upload to a signed report — not taps per screen.

points.head: One object, three views
points.body: Patient, centre and radiologist read the same case from different angles.

points.head: The failure I design against
points.body: A study that exists in the system but belongs to nobody.

sections.label: Research
sections.title: Three people, one bottleneck seen from three sides
paras: I built the research around three primary personas drawn from interviews: a hospital physician who wants accurate reads without adding to her radiologists’ workload; a rural clinic owner who wants his patients to get the same quality of interpretation as patients in the capital; and a high-volume urban hospital where delay comes from throughput rather than expertise.

Their goals converge and their obstacles do not. The physician’s blocker is coordination with external radiologists. The rural owner’s is connectivity and setup. The large hospital’s is volume and cost. Mapping their journeys across awareness, consideration and decision showed the same pattern each time: interest is easy, trust is the hard part — scepticism about a new platform, doubt about integration with existing systems, resistance from staff, worry about cost.

A competitive analysis of the remote-reading tools already in use benchmarked accessibility, speed and responsiveness, information architecture and performance. Preference testing on early designs was blunt and useful: make the scan image bigger, separate the icons, define the hierarchy more sharply, add page numbers, add colour — organised is not the same as legible.

points.head: Dr Meron — hospital physician
points.body: Needs accurate reads fast without adding to in-house radiologist workload.

points.head: Tamerat — rural clinic owner
points.body: Wants urban-quality interpretation for rural patients, over an unreliable connection.

points.head: Addis Hospital — high volume
points.body: Delay is throughput, not expertise; needs advanced imaging read at speed.

points.head: What testing changed
points.body: Bigger imagery, sharper hierarchy, separated icons, paging, more colour.

tradeoffs.old: The first design treated the scan like any other record — a detail page with the image as one field among many, consistent with the rest of the system.
tradeoffs.now: Preference testing was unambiguous: the image is the record. The viewer became a dedicated surface with the study filling it and everything else demoted to a rail.

sections.label: Architecture
sections.title: One platform, four sides
paras: The platform splits by role rather than by feature. A patient app for tracking and receiving results; a health-centre console for registering the facility, uploading studies and retrieving reports; a radiologist workspace for the reading queue, comparison and reporting; and an admin side for accounts, assignment and subscription.

A site map came before any screen. It settled the questions that decide the product — who can assign a study, where payment sits in the flow, whether a report can be issued before payment clears — and let me design each surface against a shared spine rather than negotiating them against each other later.

The updated interactive prototype explores this architecture with a shared purple identity, a lighter navigation rail, explicit study status and a patient timeline. Sample data and actions illustrate the workflow; clinical image rendering, payments and production services are outside this prototype.

points.head: Patient
points.body: Mobile. Upload status, pending payment, history, the result itself.

points.head: Health centre
points.body: Desktop. Facility profile, scan upload, viewer, results, subscription.

points.head: Radiologist
points.body: Desktop. Queue, assignment, comparison, consultation, report writing.

points.head: Admin
points.body: Desktop. Users, verification, routing and platform oversight.

desktops.name: ModernAdmin
desktops.cap: Administration — study routing, search, priority filters and radiologist assignment.

sections.label: Patient app
sections.title: A case you can watch move
paras: The refreshed patient app puts scan progress first: Uploaded, In review and Report ready. Active and completed studies sit in separate tabs, and an expandable timeline makes the next step visible.
The mobile prototype includes study upload, study details, a report state, help and a profile. It uses fictional sample data; downloadable reports are explicitly marked as examples.

points.head: Progress in plain language
points.body: Text labels and a timeline explain status alongside colour.

points.head: One clear next step
points.body: Upload a study or open its details without navigating a dashboard.

mobiles.name: ModernHome
mobiles.cap: 01 — Home. A calm overview with scan progress.

mobiles.name: ModernUploads
mobiles.cap: 02 — Upload. File requirements and referral context in one flow.

mobiles.name: ModernScansPending
mobiles.cap: 03 — Studies. Active scans and an expandable timeline.

mobiles.name: ModernResultDetail
mobiles.cap: 04 — Report. Clear availability and a labelled sample download.

sections.label: Health centre
sections.title: Upload is the moment the platform earns trust
paras: The new upload screen pairs patient and referral context with clearly stated DICOM and ZIP requirements. The study queue then gives centre staff a consistent way to find a case and follow its handoff.
The prototype keeps files in the browser session. It demonstrates submission and status changes without claiming production upload, storage or diagnostic viewing.

points.head: Constraints stated
points.body: Format, size and resolution limits shown before the upload, not after it fails.

points.head: Context at capture
points.body: Modality, patient and urgency collected with the file, never chased later.

desktops.name: ModernUploadScan
desktops.cap: Health centre — upload with patient, modality, centre and priority in one form.

desktops.name: ModernViewScan
desktops.cap: Health centre — searchable study queue with explicit assignment and report status.

sections.label: Radiologist
sections.title: A queue, two studies side by side, and a report
paras: The refreshed workspace opens on a readable study queue. Patient, centre, priority, status and assigned radiologist remain visible in the same row, with search and filters above the work.

A study detail panel holds assignment and sample reporting actions. The comparison layout explores current and prior study selection; diagnostic rendering and synchronised image controls would require a production viewer integration.

points.head: Work first
points.body: A working queue precedes summary metrics.

points.head: Visible handoffs
points.body: Assignment, review and report readiness use explicit labels.

points.head: Shared system
points.body: The desktop and patient app share purple accents, field styling and status language.

desktops.name: ModernPhyDashboard
desktops.cap: Radiologist — a clear queue for review and reporting.

desktops.name: ModernCompare
desktops.cap: Radiologist — comparison layout. Diagnostic image rendering is outside this prototype.

tradeoffs.old: An earlier radiologist dashboard opened on summary statistics — studies read this week, average turnaround, a chart. It looked like a product and was useless at 7am.
tradeoffs.now: It opens on the queue. Metrics moved to a panel the radiologist can choose to look at; the first screen answers what needs reading now.

sections.label: Design system
sections.title: A medical purple, and rules strict enough to survive four surfaces
paras: One product with four interfaces and a mixed team needs a system before it needs screens. I built the foundations as tokens — a purple brand ramp anchored on #6B42DF, neutral greys for the dense enterprise surfaces, status colours for scan states — and documented components as variant sets rather than one-off frames: buttons, form fields, checkboxes, selects, steppers, tables, cards, status chips and a full icon family.

The dense side and the consumer side share the same tokens and diverge only in density. The patient app breathes; the radiologist workspace tightens. What never changes is the meaning of a colour, the shape of a field or the position of a primary action — which is what lets a small team ship four surfaces without them drifting.

Accessibility was a design constraint rather than a review step: colour combinations and text sizes were checked against WCAG contrast, and no state is signalled by colour alone — status is always a word as well.

points.head: Tokens first
points.body: Colour, spacing and type as variables the whole team could build against.

points.head: Variants, not copies
points.body: Every component documented in its states, not its ideal.

points.head: Never colour alone
points.body: Every status carries a label — the medical requirement, not a nicety.

sections.label: Outcome
sections.title: A platform brief a team could actually build
paras: The work delivered a complete product definition — purpose, audience, market need, feature set, roadmap and team shape — alongside the research, the site map, wireframes, the four interfaces and the design system that ties them together.

Rad Reader’s premise is not technological. It is that expertise concentrated in a few places can serve the whole country if the handoff between capture and interpretation is designed properly. Everything in the product exists to make that handoff fast, accountable and legible to all three sides of it.

points.head: Shipped as a definition
points.body: Research, architecture, four interfaces and a system — enough to build from.

points.head: Next
points.body: AI-assisted triage was scoped as a later phase, deliberately after trust is established.

pm.audience: Health-centre staff, radiologists and patients following a diagnostic case.
pm.opportunity: Connect scan capture with specialist interpretation across separate organizations and locations.
pm.decision: Make the radiologist’s queue the starting point and give the scan viewer its own dedicated workspace.
pm.tradeoff: Summary statistics are useful for review, but compete with the immediate job of reading the next study. The documented design moves metrics out of the primary workflow.
pm.hypothesis: If capture, assignment, interpretation and reporting form a clear handoff, a clinic should be able to request specialist review without requiring the specialist to be on site.
pm.evidence: The portfolio documents research, preference testing, platform architecture, a product overview and a roadmap. Clinical outcomes and live turnaround improvements are not established.
metrics: Successful study upload and submission rate
Time from submitted study to completed report
Report rework and incomplete-context requests
pm.learning: A multi-sided healthcare product depends on the quality of the handoff between roles, as well as the usability of each interface.
pm.caption: Radiologist workspace: the study queue leads the reading workflow.
pm.discovery: User research with clinic staff and radiologists, followed by preference testing of the reading workspace, before the platform architecture and roadmap were set.

items.heroCaption: Rad Reader — Clinical clarity redesign. Interactive portfolio prototype with fictional sample data.

items.name: Adler Design System
items.blurb: Treating a design system as an internal product: shared foundations, findability and reusable components for a distributed team.
items.summary: A production design system: colour, typography, icon, shadow and spacing foundations, plus 40 component families documented with every state.
items.problem: A small team across three time zones kept rebuilding the same components. Consistency depended on who happened to review the work.
items.solve: Locked the foundations first — colour ramps, type scale, spacing — then documented each component state by state. An overview page lets anyone check what already exists before building it again.
did: Defined the foundations: eight-step ramps across neutral, primary, auxiliary and four semantic roles, on Ubuntu with PingFang SC for Chinese text.
Documented forty component families — Button through Upload — each with its full variant and state matrix.
Drew and catalogued a 731-icon set in line and fill themes on a shared grid.
Wrote the overview page: every family, its component count, and a preview, so the team could check before rebuilding.
Published as Figma variables and component sets so the library was consumable, not just readable.

sections.label: Problem
sections.title: Three time zones, one interface, no agreement
paras: Adler’s product was moving fast with a small distributed team. Every sprint someone needed a button, a table, an empty state — and built one. None of them were wrong on their own; together they were four products wearing the same logo.

The cost showed up as review time. Consistency was being enforced by whoever looked at the work last, which does not scale and does not survive a busy week. A system was the cheapest way to buy the team back its velocity.

points.head: Re-deciding, constantly
points.body: The same interface question answered differently each sprint.

points.head: Async makes it worse
points.body: Nobody is in the room to ask, so everyone guesses.

sections.label: Philosophy
sections.title: A system is an agreement, not a folder
paras: Component libraries fail when they are treated as storage. The value is not that a button exists somewhere — it is that everyone has agreed what a button means, when it is primary, and what it looks like while it is being pressed. The file is just where the agreement is written down.

So I documented decisions before I documented pixels. Every colour role has a stated purpose. Every component sheet leads with the rule and follows with the variants. And the overview page exists purely to answer "does this already exist?" — the question that, unanswered, is how libraries get duplicated.

points.head: What I optimise for
points.body: The number of decisions a designer does not have to make.

points.head: States, not ideals
points.body: Every component drawn hover, pressed and disabled — the states that ship wrong.

points.head: Findable beats complete
points.body: A component nobody can find gets rebuilt anyway.

tradeoffs.old: The obvious move was to start with the components the team needed that week — buttons, inputs, a table — and add foundations later once patterns emerged.
tradeoffs.now: Foundations first. Colour ramps, type scale and spacing were locked before any component was drawn, because a component built on unnamed values has to be rebuilt the moment the values get names.

sections.label: Foundations
sections.title: Eight steps of every colour, one type scale
paras: Colour is organised by role rather than by hue: neutral, primary, auxiliary, then danger, warning, success and info. Each role carries an eight-step ramp from 700 down to 50, so the same step of any role has the same visual weight — a 600 is always the pressed state, a 50 is always the faintest tint, whatever the colour.

Semantic roles carry their meaning in writing: danger for rejected or wrong, warning for in-progress, success for passed, info for no emotion at all. That last one matters — it is the role teams reach for when they want emphasis without alarm.
Typography is Ubuntu across four weights with PingFang SC for Chinese text, on a scale that stops at the sizes the product actually uses rather than a decorative range nobody types into.

points.head: Roles over hues
points.body: You pick "danger 600", never "that red".

points.head: Even steps
points.body: Ramps built so equivalent steps read at equivalent weight.

points.head: Bilingual by default
points.body: Latin and Chinese faces specified together, not retrofitted.

images.cap: Colour — eight-step ramps across neutral, primary, auxiliary and four semantic roles, with hex values.
Typography — Ubuntu and PingFang SC, weights and the working scale.

sections.label: Icons
sections.title: 731 icons that behave like one family
paras: The icon set is the part of a system most likely to drift, because icons get added under deadline. Drawing all 731 on one grid, in matched line and fill themes, made the set closable — a new icon has a shape to conform to rather than a style to invent.
They are catalogued by meaning, not by drawing: directional, suggestive, status. A designer looking for "the one that means terminated" finds it without scrolling the whole sheet.

points.head: One grid, two themes
points.body: Line and fill drawn as a pair so either can be swapped in.

points.head: Indexed by meaning
points.body: Grouped by what they communicate, not what they depict.

images.cap: The icon library — line and fill themes on a shared grid, grouped by meaning.

sections.label: Components
sections.title: Forty families, each documented state by state
paras: Every component sheet follows the same shape: the rule at the top, a copy-me instance, the variant axes, then the full state matrix. Button, for instance, states its rule plainly — one primary button per action section — then shows text-only, left-icon and right-icon across default, hover, pressed and disabled at three sizes, with the spacing specimens beside it.

Table got the most attention because it carries the most weight in an enterprise product: simple, multi-select, expandable rows, fixed columns, fixed footer and dividers, each as a worked example rather than a description. Form covers the layouts and validation states that decide whether an operator finishes a task or abandons it.
Density is the only axis allowed to vary between contexts. What never changes is the meaning of a colour, the anatomy of a field, or where the primary action sits.

points.head: Rule, then variants
points.body: Each sheet says what the component is for before showing what it can be.

points.head: A copy-me instance
points.body: The fastest correct path is also the most convenient one.

points.head: Spacing shown, not implied
points.body: Annotated specimens so implementation is not guesswork.

images.cap: Button — the rule, the variants, and the full state matrix at three sizes.
Table — simple, multi-select, expandable rows, fixed columns, fixed footer and dividers.
Form — layouts, field anatomy and validation states.

sections.label: Findability
sections.title: The overview page is the most-used screen in the system
paras: The single highest-leverage page is the inventory: every family grouped as General, Navigation, Data Entry, Data Display and Feedback, each card carrying a preview and a component count — Button 202, Input 232, Table 90, Icon 731.

It exists because the expensive failure in a design system is not a missing component, it is an unfound one. Someone who cannot see that Cascader exists builds a nested dropdown, and now there are two.

points.head: Counts on purpose
points.body: Seeing 232 input components tells you to look before you build.

points.head: Grouped by job
points.body: Data entry, data display, feedback — how designers actually search.

images.cap: The overview — every family, grouped by job, with previews and component counts.

sections.label: Outcome
sections.title: A system that outlived the sprint that needed it
paras: The library shipped as Figma variables and component sets, versioned — the file the team works in is v2.7.0, which is its own evidence: a system nobody uses does not reach a seventh minor release.

What I would watch is the same number I always watch on systems work: how often someone builds a component that already exists. That figure, not the component count, is what says whether the agreement held.

points.head: Shipped and versioned
points.body: v2.7.0 — maintained rather than published once.

points.head: The number that matters
points.body: Duplicate components built per month, trending down.

pm.audience: A distributed product design team building Adler’s social platform.
pm.opportunity: Make existing patterns findable and reusable instead of resolving consistency separately in every review.
pm.decision: Define foundations before building component families, then publish the library as variables and component sets.
pm.tradeoff: Building only the components needed this week offers immediate speed; naming shared foundations first reduces the need to revisit those components later.
pm.hypothesis: If teams can find and consume a shared component library, they should reuse more existing patterns and introduce fewer inconsistent variants.
pm.evidence: The portfolio documents 1,394 components, 731 icons and a versioned Figma library. Those are delivery outputs, not proof of faster engineering or increased adoption.
metrics: Use of library components in new product work
Duplicate or detached component creation
Time to find the right documented pattern
pm.learning: A design system needs discoverability and adoption practices; a large component count alone does not demonstrate product value.
pm.caption: Versioned design-system overview and foundation examples.

items.heroCaption: Adler design system: shared foundations and component library.

items.name: Adler Studio
items.blurb: Balancing first-session simplicity with discoverable precision in a browser-based 3D creation and publishing tool.
items.summary: Creators place architecture and furniture, tune each object numerically, add spatial audio, then publish a space others can explore.
items.problem: 3D authoring tools assume you already know 3D, so most creators never get past the first session.
items.solve: Split the tool in two: a nearly empty canvas with two gestures for composing, and a properties panel holding the exact values. Easy to start, precise enough to stay.
did: Designed the studio shell: item library, canvas and properties panel, and the rules for what lives in each.
Designed precision object controls — scale, position, rotation, texture, grouping and z-order.
Designed the audio system, from the music library to per-space playlists and spatial placement.
Designed the publish path: space management, draft and published states, and the immersive public preview.

sections.label: Problem
sections.title: 3D tools are built for people who already know 3D
paras: Spatial authoring tools inherit their vocabulary from professional 3D software: gizmos, hierarchies, modifier stacks. Adler’s users are creators and brands who want a room, not a rig.
The design problem is not simplification. It is deciding which precision to keep — because a creator who cannot set an exact dimension eventually leaves.

points.head: Two hands
points.body: Direct manipulation for composing, numeric fields for finishing. Both, not one.

sections.label: Philosophy
sections.title: Simplify the gesture, never the ceiling
paras: Most "easy" creative tools buy their simplicity by taking capability away, and the users who stay longest are exactly the ones who hit that ceiling first. I do not think approachability and precision are a trade — they are two moments in the same session.

The rule I designed to: the canvas holds the smallest possible number of gestures, and the panel holds every exact value. A beginner never meets a number they did not ask for; an expert never meets a limit they cannot type past.

points.head: What I optimise for
points.body: Time from opening the tool to something worth publishing.

points.head: The failure I design against
points.body: A creator who outgrows the product in a week.

sections.label: Scene builder
sections.title: A library on the left, the room in the middle, its properties on the right
paras: Items are grouped the way a person furnishes a space — architectural, furniture, decorative, lighting, electronics — and searchable when the list gets long. The canvas keeps an orbit cube and a hint line, so the two gestures that matter are always discoverable.
The properties panel treats a space as an object with a name, a description, real dimensions, a skybox and a soundtrack. Naming and describing a room early is what makes it publishable later.

images.cap: 3D scene builder — item library, canvas, space properties

tradeoffs.old: An early version hid all numeric fields behind an "advanced" disclosure to keep the panel calm. Testers assumed the precision did not exist and worked around it by eyeballing scale, then complained the tool was imprecise.
tradeoffs.now: Scale, position and rotation sit in the panel as three tabs, visible by default. The panel is busier; the tool is trusted. Hidden precision reads as absent precision.

sections.label: Object controls
sections.title: Every element movable, scalable, and exact
paras: Selecting an object gives a floating action bar for the frequent operations and a properties panel for the exact ones: texture with its resolution, lock state, XYZ across scale, position and rotation, plus duplicate, group, bring to front and delete.
The same panel handles the space and the object, so there is one place to look regardless of what is selected.

images.cap: Precision object controls — texture, lock, XYZ, grouping

sections.label: Audio
sections.title: Music defines how a space feels
paras: The audio system treats sound as part of the composition, not a setting. A music library with moods, genres and uploads, a per-space playlist, and spatial placement so audio has a position in the room.
Tracks carry waveform previews and durations, because choosing a soundtrack is a listening task, not a naming task.

points.head: Spatially aware
points.body: Audio positioned in 3D space for depth and realism.

points.head: Curated or custom
points.body: A rich library, or the creator’s own uploads.

images.cap: Immersive audio — music library, playlist and spatial placement

sections.label: Publish
sections.title: Manage spaces, then hand one to the public
paras: Space management is a working grid: published and draft tabs, categories, sort, view toggles, per-space views and collaborators — and a destructive-action dialog that says plainly what cannot be undone.
The public preview is the payoff. A rendered space with its author, description, tags, view count and the social loop — like, comment, share, remix — plus navigation that stays out of the room.

images.cap: Space management — published and draft spaces, delete confirmation
Immersive preview — the published space with its social loop

sections.label: Reflection
sections.title: Restraint in the canvas, generosity in the panel
paras: The pattern that made this work was keeping the canvas almost empty and letting the panels carry the complexity. Creators compose with gestures and finish with numbers, and neither group had to give anything up.

pm.audience: Creators composing and publishing browser-based 3D spaces.
pm.opportunity: Make a first scene approachable without removing the precision creators need as their work becomes more complex.
pm.decision: Keep composition on the canvas and expose precise object values in the properties panel.
pm.tradeoff: Hiding numeric controls makes the panel quieter, but makes precision harder to discover. The documented iteration keeps scale, position and rotation visible.
pm.hypothesis: If simple composition and visible precision controls coexist, creators should be able to start quickly and refine their scenes without changing tools.
pm.evidence: The case study documents scene building, object controls, audio and publishing flows, including an iteration on control visibility. Activation and retention are not quantified.
metrics: First-session completion of a usable scene
Time from first object to published preview
Successful discovery and use of precision controls
pm.learning: Progressive disclosure should not hide a capability that users need to trust the product.
pm.caption: Scene builder: object library, canvas and precision properties.

items.heroCaption: Scene builder: object library, canvas and precision properties.

items.name: Addis Park
items.blurb: A parking concept focused on certainty before commitment: map-based discovery, visible total pricing and clear session status.
items.summary: Drivers find nearby parking, reserve a space, watch the active session, and manage vehicles and payments in one app.
items.problem: Drivers had no way to know whether a space was free, what it cost, or how long they could keep it.
items.solve: Made every cost visible before it is charged: live availability and rates per lot, the total shown on the button, and a running fee during the session.
did: Designed the end-to-end parking journey: discovery, booking review, live session and account.
Built the visual system — cyan gradient headers, electric lime actions, deep navy type, 16px radii, 48–56px touch targets.
Set one navigation model across the app: Home, Map, Park, Sessions, Account.
Prepared the presentation frames and walkthrough used to pitch the concept.

sections.label: Problem
sections.title: Parking in Addis is negotiated, not booked
paras: Drivers circle. Availability is discovered by arriving, price is discovered by asking, and the transaction is cash to whoever is standing at the entrance. Nothing about the process is knowable in advance.
That produces two costs at once: time lost to searching, and no record of what was paid for what.

points.head: No advance certainty
points.body: You cannot know a space exists until you are already there.

points.head: No receipt
points.body: Cash and a spoken rate leave nothing to check afterwards.

sections.label: Philosophy
sections.title: Certainty before convenience
paras: The instinct with a parking app is to make booking fast. I think that is the second problem. The first is that a driver does not believe a space will be there — and speed applied to a promise nobody trusts just gets you to disappointment sooner.

So every screen in Addis Park is built to answer a doubt rather than save a tap: is there room, what will it cost, where exactly is my car, and what happens if I am late. Where those two goals conflicted, I chose the answer over the shortcut every time.

points.head: What I optimise for
points.body: The number of unanswered questions on screen — not the number of steps.

points.head: How I know it worked
points.body: A second booking. Nobody re-books a service they had to gamble on.

sections.label: Discovery
sections.title: A map that answers three questions at a glance
paras: The map opens on the nearest verified lot with the only three numbers that matter — distance, spots available and the rate. A verified badge separates managed lots from informal ones.
Trust cues sit below the fold, not in the hero: secure parking, time saved, cashless payment, support. Reassurance where a hesitant first-time user looks for it.

points.head: Rate in the card
points.body: Price is part of discovery, not something revealed at checkout.

images.cap: Parking discovery — map, nearest verified lot, spots and rate

tradeoffs.old: The first discovery screen was list-first, sorted by distance — faster to scan and easier to build. In testing nobody could tell whether a lot was on their route, which is the actual decision being made.
tradeoffs.now: The map leads, with a single nearest-lot card docked below it. One recommendation on a map beats ten rows without one.

sections.label: Booking
sections.title: State the total before you take the money
paras: The booking review lays out the lot, vehicle, date, arrival time and duration plan, then itemises the cost: parking fee, service fee, EV charging if added, total. The primary action names the amount — "Reserve for 60 Birr".
Free cancellation up to an hour before arrival sits directly under the button, because the fear being managed is commitment, not payment.

points.head: EV as an option, not a tier
points.body: Charging is a toggle inside the same booking rather than a separate product.

points.head: The button states the price
points.body: No screen between the number and the confirmation.

images.cap: Booking review — itemised payment summary and priced action

sections.label: Session
sections.title: While parked, one number matters
paras: The active session screen is built around the countdown and the fee accruing against it, with the vehicle, lot and exact spot above so a driver returning can find their car.
Two actions only: extend time, or end parking. Extend is primary because it is the one people need in a hurry.

points.head: The countdown and the fee together
points.body: Time remaining answers "can I stay", the accruing fee answers "should I". Separating them makes a driver do arithmetic in a car park.

points.head: Extend is the primary action
points.body: Ending parking happens when you are already walking back. Extending happens under pressure, from a meeting that ran long — so it gets the weight.

points.head: Spot before status
points.body: Lot, floor and bay sit above the timer, because the first thing a returning driver needs is to find the car, not to read a receipt.

images.cap: Active session — time remaining, current fee, extend or end

sections.label: Account
sections.title: Vehicle, balance and history in one place
paras: The account holds the parking balance with a top-up entry point, the saved vehicle and plate, the saved card, and the settings a returning user actually opens: transaction history, notifications, language, security, help.

Everything here exists to make the second booking shorter than the first. A saved plate and a saved card turn a five-field checkout into a confirmation, which is the whole retention argument for a service used twice a day.

points.head: Balance in vouchers
points.body: Top-up sits on the balance itself, so the moment a driver notices they are short is the moment they can fix it.

points.head: The plate is the account
points.body: Vehicle and plate persist and are shown plainly — attendants ask for the plate, so the app leads with it.

points.head: History as reassurance
points.body: Transaction history is the top settings row: for a cash-replacing product, the record is the trust mechanism.

images.cap: Account — balance, vehicle, saved payment and settings

sections.label: Design system
sections.title: One family of decisions, applied everywhere
paras: Bright cyan gradients for branded headers, electric lime for primary actions and selected states, deep navy typography and a single rounded outline-icon family.
White cards, cool-grey shadows, 16px radii, 24px margins and 48–56px touch targets throughout — the constraints that let five screens read as one app.

points.head: One navigation model
points.body: Home, Map, Park, Sessions, Account — identical placement on every screen.

points.head: Lime means action
points.body: The accent is reserved for the primary action and the selected state, never decoration.

images.cap: The system applied across the five screens

pm.audience: Drivers choosing, reserving and paying for parking in Addis Ababa.
pm.opportunity: Reduce uncertainty about location, availability, price and the active parking session.
pm.decision: Lead with a map and show the complete price before a booking is confirmed.
pm.tradeoff: A nearby-lot list is straightforward to scan, but location relative to the route matters. The documented direction uses a map with a recommended lot.
pm.hypothesis: If drivers can understand the location and total cost before committing, they should be more confident completing a parking reservation.
pm.evidence: The case study contains a concept, end-to-end flows, presentation frames and documented design decisions. It does not establish a live launch or booking conversion.
metrics: Completion of a find-and-reserve usability task
Comprehension of the total price before confirmation
Successful extension and ending of an active session
pm.learning: For an unfamiliar service, clear pricing and location can be more important than shortening the flow by one step.
